claims.text: Combining machine-learned interatomic potentials with thermodynamic integration can determine melting temperatures and fusion, volume-change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
The machine-learned interatomic potentials can accurately capture the complex interatomic interactions in high-entropy alloys.
Thermodynamic integration along a defined melting pathway quantifies free-energy changes, latent heat, and volume change.
High-throughput sampling can overcome challenges associated with configurational complexity in high-entropy systems.
Local atomic rearrangements and cluster reorganization at melting mediate changes in enthalpy, entropy, and volume.
The proposed approach will predict melting temperatures within 5% of experimental values.
The proposed approach will estimate enthalpies of fusion with errors of approximately ±10%.
The proposed approach will estimate entropies of fusion with errors of approximately ±10%.
The proposed approach will reliably determine volume changes at melting.
The proposed approach will consistently describe liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a diverse set of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
Conventional interatomic potentials are less accurate because of oversimplified potential forms.
Direct ab initio molecular dynamics is computationally expensive for systematic exploration across compositions.
The approach is applicable when its machine-learned potential has been validated against density-functional-theory data over the relevant alloy domain.
The approach is applicable to simulations containing hundreds to a few thousand atoms and alloys of moderate chemical complexity.
The approach is expected to work when melting is governed primarily by local rearrangements rather than long-range phase separation or ordering absent from the training data.
Extreme chemical or structural inhomogeneity may limit extrapolation of the approach.
Incomplete transferability to liquid-state chemical short-range order, inadequate molecular-dynamics sampling, and density-functional-theory calibration errors may degrade the predictions.
